extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers; journalists and newspaper advertisers/editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards embedded in a wartime newspaper piece covering press responsibilities, reader judgement, military communiqués, POW treatment, advertising practice, and consumer/travel tips for Americans abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with Geneva Convention for POWs
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment of prisoners of war must comply with the Geneva Convention; chaining or fettering prisoners is a breach (the Germans 'violated regulation two' by chaining up prisoners taken at Dieppe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representations should be made via protecting powers (Switzerland) to protest breaches; governments may urge the offending power to desist and can withdraw countermeasures if it does. Public discussion that could prejudice protecting-power action is discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reprisal measures against POW mistreatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Reprisal measures (e.g., fettering enemy prisoners) are not generally countenanced by government policy but 'may, from time to time, under the stress of circumstances, be necessary' and may be regarded as in the interests of prisoners' safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such measures should be considered exceptional; governments should lodge formal protests and seek remedy through protecting powers, and withdraw reprisals if the offending party desists.

rubrics_metrics.name: News agencies' responsibility to supply truthful, impartial reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: News agencies have a responsibility to give the papers they serve the truth and to be 'independent, impartial' so as to ensure the permanence of peace and public understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain integrity, independence and freedom from bias at all times (as urged by the Reuters trust); news organizations should cover all portions of the globe and preserve objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader guidance: judge the news and follow reliable sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should 'judge the news' and habitually follow sources proven to be 'not necessarily the most exciting or most pleasant, but the most reliable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 'the simplest critical faculty' when selecting news sources; prefer reliability over sensationalism to help preserve truth in news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military communiqué transparency and separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Military headquarters should issue regular, clear communiqués about operations (example: Maj. Gen. Maxwell announced issuing daily communiqués separate from British Army and RAF reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide separate, regular updates to improve clarity of operations; differentiate national/hq-level reporting when appropriate so audiences can understand separate theaters/commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combat reporting: use precise qualifiers for battle damage/losses
rubrics_metrics.description: Combat reports distinguish between 'definitely destroyed', 'probably', and 'so badly damaged that some probably never regained their bases' when reporting enemy losses (e.g., '47 definitely destroyed and about 50... so badly damaged...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report losses with qualifiers and time/place context (daylight vs. night, three-day totals etc.), and avoid asserting unconfirmed enemy claims; note discrepancies when other sources disagree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wartime newspaper advertising allocation and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Wartime conditions changed advertising: advertising now fills about 23% of newspaper space (government may take a nominal 25% of available space); ad sizes reduced and content shifted toward institutional, goodwill, or prestige advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers may focus on prestige/institutional messages rather than product volume; newspapers should manage limited newsprint and prioritize government space allocations while explaining constrained availability to readers/advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper circulation and distribution constraints in wartime
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper circulation and street sales are limited by newsprint shortages and allocation rules; supplies to stations, subways, hotels are quickly exhausted and some papers cannot supply additional copies despite demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors/managers should communicate shortages to readers, employ extra staff to handle inquiries, and prioritize distribution channels given constrained resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer verification tips when buying souvenirs abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical checks advised for Americans buying jewelry and carvings overseas: test a ruby by soaking it in water overnight to see if water turns red; have purchases appraised at a reputable (English) shop; ensure a carved African bust advertised as ebony is actually ebony and not cheaper ironwood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, local tests and reputable appraisal before purchase; when satisfied, send valuable purchases home via Army/official post to reduce risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health precaution for travelers/servicemen (malaria prophylaxis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Travelers and troops abroad should guard against malaria and tropical alimentary illnesses (references to 'Teheran tummy', 'Delhi belly', 'Kunming colic') and 'take a five-in-quinine pill' after certain exposures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt prophylactic measures (quinine where indicated), be cautious with native-cooked foods, and follow medical guidance to reduce risk of malaria and febrile stomach illnesses while overseas.
